request: what does a 2x2 matrix actually do to the unit square?

beats.intent: The grid with i-hat, j-hat and the yellow unit square
beats.narration: Start with the unit square, sitting on the two basis vectors i-hat and j-hat.
beats.code:
stage.title("A matrix meets the unit square")
p = draw_plane(stage)
sq = draw_unit_square(stage, p)
i_hat, j_hat = draw_basis(stage, p)
stage.caption("One by one, resting on i-hat and j-hat")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The whole grid tilting as the square becomes a parallelogram
beats.narration: Apply the matrix with columns (2, 0.5) and (1, 1.5). The square rides along and becomes a parallelogram.
beats.code:
apply_matrix(stage, p, [[2, 1], [0.5, 1.5]], riders=[sq, i_hat, j_hat])
stage.caption("i-hat lands on (2, 0.5), j-hat on (1, 1.5)")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The matrix written beside the parallelogram, its columns as the new edges
beats.narration: The two columns of the matrix are exactly the two edges of the new shape.
beats.code:
eq = stage.equation(r"\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0.5 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix}", where="right")
highlight(stage, sq)
stage.caption("Columns = where the square's edges go")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The parallelogram's area read off as the determinant, 2.5
beats.narration: Its area is the determinant: two times one and a half, minus one times a half, which is two and a half.
beats.code:
stage.play(FadeOut(eq))
stage.equation(r"\det = 2 \cdot 1.5 - 1 \cdot 0.5", r"\det = 2.5", where="right")
pulse(stage, sq)
stage.caption("Area 1 becomes area 2.5")
stage.pause(1)

request: show me the eigenvectors of a stretch along the diagonal y = x

beats.intent: The lines y = x and y = -x, with a vector on each and a red one along the x-axis
beats.narration: Draw the two diagonals, put a vector on each, and one more red vector along the x-axis.
beats.code:
stage.title("Stretching along y = x")
p = draw_plane(stage)
d1 = draw_span(stage, p, (1, 1), color=BLUE)
d2 = draw_span(stage, p, (1, -1), color=TEAL)
v = draw_vector(stage, p, (1, 1), color=YELLOW, label="v")
w = draw_vector(stage, p, (1, -1), color=GREEN, label="w")
u = draw_vector(stage, p, (1, 0), color=RED, label="u")
stage.caption("Two diagonal lines and three test vectors")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The plane stretched three times along y = x; v and w stay on their lines, u tips off
beats.narration: This matrix stretches the plane by three along the diagonal. v stays on its line and triples, w does not move, but u is knocked off the x-axis.
beats.code:
apply_matrix(stage, p, [[2, 1], [1, 2]], riders=[v, w, u])
stage.caption("v triples, w stays put, u turns to (2, 1)")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The matrix and its two eigen-equations beside the stretched grid
beats.narration: Vectors that stay on their own line are eigenvectors: v with eigenvalue three, w with eigenvalue one.
beats.code:
stage.equation(r"A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}", r"A\vec{v} = 3\vec{v} \\ A\vec{w} = 1\,\vec{w}", where="right")
pulse(stage, v)
stage.caption("Eigenvalues 3 and 1")
stage.pause(1)

request: why do some vectors just get longer when you apply a matrix, without turning?

beats.intent: The grid moving and knocking (1, 1) off its line to (4, 2)
beats.narration: Apply the matrix three, one, zero, two. The vector lands at four, two, off its old line: it turned.
beats.code:

stage.caption("v = (1, 1) lands at (4, 2): it turned")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: A fresh grid where two yellow vectors stay on their lines while a red one turns
beats.narration: But some directions are special. Along the x-axis and along the line y equals minus x, vectors only stretch.

p2 = draw_plane(stage, where="left")
riders = show_eigenvectors(stage, p2, [[3, 1], [0, 2]])

beats.intent: The two stretch factors written beside the grid
beats.narration: Along the x-axis everything triples; along y equals minus x everything doubles. Those are the eigenvectors.

request: explain the dot product as how much two arrows agree

beats.intent: v leaning along w, casting a long green shadow on w's line
beats.narration: Drop v's shadow onto w's line. When they point roughly the same way, the shadow is long.
beats.code:
stage.title("How much do they agree?")
p = draw_plane(stage)
v, w, s = project_vector(stage, p, (2, 1), (3, 0))
stage.caption("Shadow 2 times length 3: v·w = 6")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: v standing upright at a right angle to w, with no shadow
beats.narration: Stand v straight up, at a right angle to w. There is no shadow at all: the dot product is zero.
beats.code:
stage.clear(keep=[p])
v2, w2, s2 = project_vector(stage, p, (0, 2), (3, 0))
stage.caption("At right angles: v·w = 0")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: v pointing back against w, its shadow on the negative side
beats.narration: Point v backwards and the shadow falls behind the origin. They disagree, so the dot product is negative.
beats.code:
stage.clear(keep=[p])
v3, w3, s3 = project_vector(stage, p, (-2, 1), (3, 0))
stage.caption("Pointing against w: v·w = -6")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The cosine formula beside the backward-pointing pair
beats.narration: In general the dot product is the two lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
beats.code:
stage.equation(r"\vec{v}\cdot\vec{w} = |\vec{v}|\,|\vec{w}|\cos\theta", where="right")
stage.caption("The cosine measures the agreement")
stage.pause(1)

request: what happens in gradient descent if the learning rate is way too small

beats.intent: A bowl-shaped loss curve with its minimum marked at w = 2
beats.narration: Here is a loss curve shaped like a bowl, lowest at w equals two.
beats.code:
stage.title("A tiny learning rate")
ax = draw_axes(stage, x_range=(-1, 5), y_range=(0, 5), labels=("w", r"\text{loss}"))
f = lambda x: 0.5 * (x - 2) ** 2
g = plot_graph(stage, ax, f)
low = mark_point(stage, ax, (2, 0), color=GREEN, label="minimum")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: A yellow ball taking twelve tiny steps from w = -0.5, still far from the bottom
beats.narration: Start at minus a half with a learning rate of 0.03. Each step is tiny, and after twelve steps the ball has barely moved.
beats.code:
ball = gradient_descent(stage, ax, f, -0.5, lr=0.03, steps=12)
stage.caption("Rate 0.03: twelve steps, still far away")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: An orange ball with a bigger rate landing at the bottom in six steps
beats.narration: From the same start with a rate of 0.5, the ball reaches the bottom in six steps.
beats.code:
ball2 = gradient_descent(stage, ax, f, -0.5, lr=0.5, steps=6, color=ORANGE)
stage.caption("Rate 0.5: at the bottom in six steps")
stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: The update rule beside the two balls
beats.narration: Every step moves by the learning rate times the slope. Make the rate tiny and every step is tiny too.
beats.code:
stage.equation(r"w_{n+1} = w_n - \eta\, f'(w_n)", where="right")
stage.caption("Small eta: small steps, slow progress")
stage.pause(1)

request: show how rectangles under a curve get closer to the area when you use more of them

stage.pause(1)

beats.intent: Four wide rectangles under the curve leaving gaps
beats.narration: Four rectangles, each one wide, give 7.5. They leave gaps under the curve.

rects = riemann_refine(stage, ax, g, 0, 4, ns=(4,))

beats.intent: The rectangles splitting into 8, 16, 32 and 64 thinner strips

beats.intent: A small angle on a circle where the arc and the vertical height almost match

stage.label(h, "sin x", direction=LEFT, color=GREEN)
stage.caption("Small angle: height is almost the arc")
